competitors.name: TridentSec (PSIRT-as-a-Service)
competitors.what_they_do: Boutique consultancy selling a monthly PSIRT-as-a-Service retainer for connected-device makers: triage, CVE assignment, researcher relations, advisory publishing and 'ENISA coordination', with SLA-backed response times. Also sells a Fractional PSIRT Lead retainer. The site does not claim 24/7 coverage or publish prices.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Small one-founder consultancy (Kris Barcewicz). No funding disclosed.

competitors.name: Finite State (managed CRA service)
competitors.what_they_do: Product-security platform with a 12-month managed CRA service: living SBOM from firmware binaries, continuous monitoring against 250+ intel sources, analyst prioritisation and disclosure calls, and draft 24h/72h/14d notifications. Aimed at teams with 'one or two people in product security, or no dedicated function'. Filing stays customer-owned and no 24/7 coverage is stated.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Venture-backed US product-security vendor. I did not verify funding figures. Pricing is not published.

competitors.name: Cybellum (managed PSIRT / incident response service)
competitors.what_they_do: Product-security vendor with a service for outsourcing post-production monitoring, triage and analysis, run by product-security staff plus AI. It is pitched at manufacturers who want to outsource post-production risk management and lists EU CRA among the regulations. Positioned for automotive, medical and industrial enterprises. I could not load the page directly, so this comes from search snippets.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Venture-funded enterprise vendor. Funding not verified.

competitors.name: Patchstack (managed CRA Article 14 reporting for open source)
competitors.what_they_do: Launched 11 Sep 2026. Free service that tracks exploited vulnerabilities, collects evidence and acts as the Assigned Representative to file Article 14 reports on the SRP for open-source stewards and maintainers. It shows the 'we file for you' model is legal and already being productised. It targets open source, not hardware makers.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Established WordPress and open-source security company. Says it covers 1,000+ OSS products and projects. Currently free, per-report fee possible later.

competitors.name: CVD Portal
competitors.what_they_do: SaaS for CRA compliance: white-label vulnerability intake portal, Article 14 workflow with 24h/72h/14d timers, SBOM registry, EUVD/NVD feeds and technical-file generation. Prices run from a free tier to EUR 99/mo (Reporting) and EUR 299/mo (Compliance). The final SRP filing stays a human action by the manufacturer. No 24/7 human service.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Unknown, apparently small. Published pricing anchors software-only reporting tooling at EUR 99-299/mo.

competitors.name: CRA Evidence
competitors.what_they_do: CRA compliance platform covering SBOM/HBOM, continuous CVE monitoring with EPSS, VEX, Annex VII technical file and ENISA deadline tracking. Also sells consulting engagements, including an 'Authority/Incident Response Plan' and a Programme Lead retainer. Pricing is custom.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Unknown. Crunchbase profile exists but returned 403.

competitors.name: EcoComply (EU Authorised Representative)
competitors.what_they_do: Acts as EU Authorised Representative for non-EU manufacturers, with a mandate drafted to cover Article 14 reporting. From EUR 1,500 per product category per year. Provides the reporting counterparty, not 24/7 triage.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Small compliance startup (CEO John Iwueke). Funding not disclosed.

competitors.name: H-X Technologies
competitors.what_they_do: Consultancy offering 'CRA Article 14 Reporting Readiness': designs and tests workflows, and prepares draft notifications after technical analysis. The manufacturer or its authorised representative submits.
competitors.scale_or_funding: European multi-domain compliance consultancy. Size not disclosed.

competitors.name: SBOM/monitoring tool vendors (Seentrix, Zealience, Regulus, CRACI, ONEKEY, Cybeats)
competitors.what_they_do: Software that ingests SBOMs, monitors CVEs and generates CRA documentation. Seentrix (https://seentrix.com/blog/vulnerability-disclosure-setting-up-your-first-psirt) explicitly sells monitoring feeding a PSIRT. Others: https://zealience.com/cyber-resilience-act-compliance/ , https://goregulus.com/ , https://www.onekey.com/ , https://www.cybeats.com/ . These commoditise the SBOM-matching layer of the idea.
competitors.scale_or_funding: CRACI (Helsinki) raised a EUR 1.4M pre-seed led by Lifeline Ventures. ONEKEY and Cybeats are funded. Others unknown.

competitors.name: Large MSSPs and certification bodies (Kudelski Security, Bureau Veritas/Secura, TUV SUD, DEKRA)
competitors.what_they_do: Kudelski sells 24x7 incident-response retainers and a managed SOC. Bureau Veritas/Secura, TUV SUD and DEKRA sell CRA gap analysis, testing and conformity advice. None was found marketing a CRA PSIRT desk. Each could add a retainer quickly and already owns the relationships with the target customers.

white_space:
The genuinely unserved piece is a contractually guaranteed 24/7 desk that files as the client's named Assigned Representative on the SRP, priced for 20-500 person device makers.
- Nobody found sells this in that form. TridentSec sells operations with no stated 24/7 and no published price. Finite State and H-X draft the notice but leave filing to the customer. Cybellum's service targets enterprises. CVD Portal, CRA Evidence and other tools stop at timers and packages, and their final filing is a human step by the customer. Patchstack files as AR but only for open source, and free.
- The intake step is also unserved: nobody takes weekend and night hits on 'is this KEV/EUVD entry in our firmware' and makes the call inside the 24h window.

What is not white space:
- The SBOM-to-CVE matching layer is commoditised. CVD Portal's Reporting tier is EUR 99/mo, and CRACI, Zealience, Regulus and ONEKEY sell the same thing.
- Boutiques and large consultancies can add 'PSIRT retainer' as a line item in weeks.
- The idea's claim that there is 'almost no visible tooling' is wrong. The service layer is thin, but the tooling layer is crowded.

Structural problems to plan around:
- The CRA fine exemption for micro and small enterprises on the 24h deadline (Art 64(10), https://cra-facts.com/penalties) removes the sharpest fear driver for the smallest customers. The 72h and 14-day deadlines still carry fines up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover.
- The SRP requires each AR to use a personal EU Login with MFA (https://www.enisa.europa.eu/topics/product-security/single-reporting-platform-srp/frequently-asked-questions), so named analysts must sit in the loop.
- Liability stays with the manufacturer, and the desk needs professional indemnity cover.
- The 24h clock starts when the manufacturer becomes aware, so a desk that spots an exploit may start the client's clock.
- An actively exploited vulnerability in one specific product's components is a low-frequency event. The retainer therefore risks being seen as insurance that customers only buy under audit pressure.
evidence_of_demand:
Real but soft and mostly supply-side. I found no RFPs, forum complaints from named small makers, or published customer counts.

Regulatory push (strong):
- Article 14 reporting applied from 11 Sep 2026 and the ENISA SRP went live the same day. Fines run up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of turnover. See https://www.crowell.com/en/insights/client-alerts/its-live-the-cyber-resilience-act-reporting-is-mandatory-as-of-today-11-september-2026 and https://cra-facts.com/penalties.
- Law-firm and press coverage stresses that firms need a PSIRT-like process and that 24h is tight. See https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/09/11/eus-cyber-resilience-act-starts-the-24-hour-vulnerability-clock/5295821 (which says the pain is supply-chain visibility, not staffing), https://startupfortune.com/eus-cyber-resilience-act-now-requires-24-hour-hack-reporting/ and https://www.fisherphillips.com/en/insights/insights/eu-cyber-resilience-act-reporting-is-now-live.
- An ENISA survey reported via a Mondaq/UpGuard search result found 66% of SME respondents had heard of the CRA and one in five were unsure it applied to them.

Vendors are already building for it:
- Finite State markets its managed service to teams with 'one or two people in product security, or no dedicated function' (https://finitestate.io/blog/cra-compliance-is-a-full-time-job).
- TridentSec sells a PSIRT-as-a-Service retainer (https://tridentsec.eu/services/psirt-consulting/).
- Patchstack launched free managed Article 14 filing for OSS on day one (https://patchstack.com/articles/launching-managed-cra-article-14-reporting-for-open-source-maintainers/).
- CRACI raised a EUR 1.4M pre-seed for CRA automation (https://arcticstartup.com/craci-raises-e1-4-million-pre-seed/).

Price anchors:
- EcoComply charges from EUR 1,500 per product category per year for an authorised-representative mandate covering Article 14 (https://ecocomply.ai/blog/cra-reporting-obligations-non-eu-manufacturers).
- CVD Portal charges EUR 99-299/mo for software (https://cvdportal.com/pricing).
- Outsourced-DPO services are a comparable model at EUR 1,500-5,000/mo mid-range (https://www.engagecompliance.co/outsourced-dpo-cost-guide).
- Regulus's calculator estimates only 16-32 hours (about EUR 1.4-2.7k) of internal effort to set up vulnerability handling and reporting readiness (https://goregulus.com/resources/cra-cost-calculator/). That suggests many small firms will do it in-house at low cost.

No evidence found that anyone pays EUR 1,500-6,000/mo for a filing desk today, because the regime is only 17 days old.
sharper_angle:
Do not launch as a generic 'PSIRT retainer'. TridentSec, Finite State, Cybellum and the consultancies already own that framing, and CVD Portal has pushed software-only reporting down to EUR 99/mo. Launch instead as the 24/7 Article 14 filing desk for non-EU connected-device brands, with three changes.

1. Bundle the AR mandate with the filing SLA. Be the named SRP Assigned Representative plus EU authorised-representative mandate, with a written guarantee such as 'triage decision within 4h, early warning filed inside 24h including weekends'. That is the one deliverable competitors avoid because filing is 'customer-owned'. Price it as a low base fee (EUR 300-800/mo or EUR 2-4k/yr per product family, anchored to EcoComply's EUR 1,500/yr AR price) plus a per-incident fee (EUR 1-3k). Do not price it at EUR 1,500-6,000/mo up front.

2. Pool the triage by shared component stack, not by client. Specialise in a few stacks that many small makers share: ESP-IDF/ESP32, OpenWrt/Qualcomm and Realtek router SDKs, Zephyr, Tuya and Matter modules, and Yocto Linux. An actively exploited entry in one SDK then gets analysed once and fanned out to 30-100 clients as pre-approved VEX and notice drafts. That is where the 30-clients-per-analyst economics come from, and it is hard for one-off consultancies to copy.

3. Sell through channels that carry the liability, not to the makers directly. Target EU importers and marketplace sellers, ODM/contract manufacturers, and chip and module vendors' ecosystems. Also offer white-label wholesale 24/7 back-end capacity to TUV, DEKRA, Bureau Veritas, TridentSec and the SBOM platforms, so incumbents become distributors, not rivals.

Sequencing: sell the audit and drill first as the lead product, since reporting-readiness is what regulators and customers will ask for. Treat the monthly filing desk as the recurring add-on, and expect it to sell mainly to firms above the small-enterprise fine exemption (50+ staff or over EUR 10M turnover). Move fast: Patchstack shows platforms can ship managed filing within days, so the window before this becomes a checkbox feature is probably 6-12 months. Before committing, get a professional-indemnity quote and confirm with ENISA or a CSIRT that an external firm can serve as AR using personal EU Login accounts.
